bash-eval-call.problem: eval takes a string and runs it as a fresh shell command. Whatever ends up in that string — including content from a file, an environment variable, or a network response — is executed.
bash-eval-call.impact: Anyone who can influence the string can run arbitrary commands as the user running the script. This is full local code execution.
bash-eval-call.fix: Avoid eval. If you need to call a command stored in a variable, use an array: cmd=(ls -l); "${cmd[@]}". For dynamic dispatch, use a case statement against a known list of allowed actions.

bash-curl-pipe-bash.problem: curl ... | bash downloads a script and runs it immediately. The shell trusts whatever bytes the server returns and runs them with your user's privileges.
bash-curl-pipe-bash.impact: If the server is compromised, hijacked, or simply MITM'd over plain HTTP, an attacker gets arbitrary code execution on the machine running the pipe.
bash-curl-pipe-bash.fix: Download the script first, verify its checksum or signature, then execute it: curl -fsSL https://example.com/install.sh -o install.sh && sha256sum -c install.sh.sha256 && bash install.sh.

bash-unquoted-var-rm.problem: rm -rf $DIR splits the variable on whitespace, expands glob characters, and may expand to nothing at all if the variable is empty. If $DIR is empty, the command becomes rm -rf (no target); if it contains spaces, multiple paths are deleted; if it starts with a dash, it is parsed as a flag.
bash-unquoted-var-rm.impact: Mass deletion of unintended files, or in the worst case rm -rf / when the variable is empty. Very common cause of catastrophic data loss in CI scripts.
bash-unquoted-var-rm.fix: Always quote: rm -rf -- "$DIR". The -- prevents dashes in $DIR from being parsed as flags, and the double quotes prevent word-splitting and globbing.

bash-sudo-no-password.problem: sudo -n runs sudo non-interactively — it will fail rather than prompt for a password. This pattern is typically used because a passwordless sudoers entry exists for the user.
bash-sudo-no-password.impact: If the script or any program it calls can be tampered with, an attacker can escalate to root without needing a credential. The blast radius of any compromise increases significantly.
bash-sudo-no-password.fix: Drop the passwordless sudo entry from /etc/sudoers.d and require interactive authentication, or narrow the sudoers rule to a single fixed command path (Cmnd_Alias) rather than a wildcard.

bash-hardcoded-password.problem: A password, API key, or token is written directly as a literal in the script. The credential lives in git history forever and is visible to anyone who can read the repository.
bash-hardcoded-password.impact: Credential leak. Anyone with read access to the repo, a backup, or a build log can use the secret to access the protected resource.
bash-hardcoded-password.fix: Load secrets from environment variables that are populated outside the repo (export PASSWORD=$(cat /run/secrets/db)), or fetch them at runtime from a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, sops, etc.).

bash-chmod-777.problem: chmod 777 grants read, write, and execute to owner, group, and everyone else. Any process on the host — including a compromised low-privilege account — can modify or replace the file.
bash-chmod-777.impact: An attacker who gets any shell on the machine can backdoor the file. If the file is a script or binary that root runs, this is a privilege escalation path.
bash-chmod-777.fix: Grant the minimum needed. For files only the owner edits: chmod 600. For files the owner writes and others read: chmod 644. For executables: chmod 755. Reserve 777 for ephemeral debug only.

bash-wget-no-https.problem: Downloading over http:// (no TLS) means anyone on the network path between the script and the server can read or modify the response. This includes ISPs, wifi hotspot operators, and anyone who tampers with DNS.
bash-wget-no-https.impact: An attacker can replace the downloaded file with a malicious version. If the script later executes the file or trusts its contents, the attacker controls what runs.
bash-wget-no-https.fix: Switch to https://. If the server does not support TLS, host the artifact somewhere that does (e.g. a CDN), and verify a sha256 checksum after download.

bash-test-string-no-quotes.problem: Inside [ ... ], unquoted variables are word-split and glob-expanded. If $X is empty, the test becomes [ = $Y ] which is a syntax error; if $X contains spaces, it is split into multiple tokens.
bash-test-string-no-quotes.impact: The script crashes on empty input or produces wrong results on input containing whitespace. In conditional logic this often takes the wrong branch silently.
bash-test-string-no-quotes.fix: Always double-quote variables inside [ ... ]: if [ "$X" = "$Y" ]. Or use the [[ ... ]] form, which does not split or glob: if [[ $X = $Y ]].

bash-todo-comment.problem: A TODO or FIXME marker indicates known incomplete or buggy code. Once it sits in the script, it stops being visible to reviewers and is rarely addressed.
bash-todo-comment.impact: Latent bugs and missing functionality stay hidden behind a comment that everyone has learned to skim past.
bash-todo-comment.fix: Move each TODO/FIXME into your issue tracker with concrete context, link to the issue from the code if a marker is still needed, and remove markers that are no longer relevant.
